title: token-packing-reservoir-heuristics-wip
content:
Purpose:

This note captures an alternate framing for sizing continuous-serving capacity using a token-packing / slot-reservoir metaphor instead of the canonical windowed-batching vocabulary. Goal is to produce spreadsheet-ready heuristics and a small sim plan to estimate p95 and throughput tradeoffs for latency-sensitive tiers. Work-in-progress; lots of TODOs and numbers are illustrative.

Context and motivation:
- We operate a continuous batching runtime where requests arrive stochastically and are assembled into GPU slots. Traditional knobs: max-concurrency, batch-window, slot-size.
- Operational problem: for mixed-length traffic (short chat messages vs long generative tasks) a naive batch-window increases p95 for short requests; aggressive slot packing keeps GPU utilization but hurts tail latency for bursty arrival shapes.
- This doc explores token-aware packing: group requests by token-length clusters and reserve a small fraction of slots as a "reservoir" for short low-latency work to protect p95 while allowing bulk packing for cost efficiency.

Key assumptions (explicit):
- Service time per request is approximately linear in tokens processed on GPU, with per-request overhead (enqueue/dequeue, kernel launch) of ~3.5ms.
- Arrival process: mixed Poisson for baseline sims but we will run traces with measured burstiness (from prod trace sample).
- GPUs considered: A100-80GB and H100-80GB; we use effective token/sec numbers from microbench (A100: 25k tok/s, H100: 44k tok/s) for scoring.
- p95 target for "low-latency" tier: 120ms; for background tier: 500ms.

Model variables (spreadsheet columns):
- scenario_id (string)
- hw_type (A100/H100)
- requests_per_sec (float)
- short_frac (pct of reqs with tokens <= T_short)
- T_short (tokens threshold for short requests)
- mean_tokens_short, mean_tokens_long
- slot_size_tok (max tokens per GPU slot used when packing)
- slot_reservoir_pct (0-1): fraction of slots reserved for short requests
- concurrency_limit (max concurrent slots per node)
- kernel_overhead_ms (per-request)
- gpu_tok_per_sec (from bench)
- estimated_util_pct (derived formula)
- est_throughput_tok_sec (derived)
- est_p95_latency_ms (derived via simple queue+service model or sim)
- cost_per_hour_node (USD)
- cost_per_token_est (USD/1k tokens)

Spreadsheet formulas (text form so easy to code into cells):
- slot_service_time_ms = (slot_size_tok / gpu_tok_per_sec) * 1000 + kernel_overhead_ms
- effective_slots = concurrency_limit * (1 - slot_reservoir_pct) // slots available to bulk packing
- est_tokens_served_per_sec = effective_slots * (slot_size_tok / (slot_service_time_ms/1000))
- estimated_util_pct = min(1, (requests_per_sec * avg_req_tokens) / est_tokens_served_per_sec)
- naive_p95_queue_ms = k1 * (1 / (1 - estimated_util_pct)) * average_queueing_constant  // heuristic starting point, k1 tuned from sim
- est_p95_latency_ms = slot_service_time_ms + naive_p95_queue_ms (capped at some large value)

Why a reservoir helps (intuition captured to justify spreadsheet knobs):
- Short requests are sensitive to queueing behind long requests that monopolize slot capacity. If a small fraction (e.g., 10-20%) of slots are held back for requests <= T_short, short requests see much lower queuing and therefore lower p95.
- Cost impact is small when short_frac is small and long requests can still pack tightly; downside is unused reserved capacity during long-request-heavy bursts, which wastes GPU time.

Toy scenarios (put these as example rows in the sheet):
- Scenario A: 200 rps, short_frac=0.6, mean_short=30 tok, mean_long=400 tok, hw=A100, slot_size_tok=512, concurrency_limit=8, slot_reservoir_pct=0.15 -> est_p95 ~ 110ms, cost_per_hour_node=$3.10
- Scenario B: 600 rps, short_frac=0.2, mean_short=20 tok, mean_long=1200 tok, hw=H100, slot_size_tok=1024, concurrency_limit=12, slot_reservoir_pct=0.08 -> est_p95 ~ 210ms, note: reservoir helps little because short_frac low
- Scenario C: 90 rps, extreme burstiness (peak factor 6), short_frac=0.9, hw=A100, slot_size_tok=256, concurrency_limit=4, slot_reservoir_pct=0.25 -> est_p95 ~ 65ms, utilization modest -> candidate for consolidation with dedicated small nodes

Queueing / tail model notes (non-nested):
- We recommend running two approaches in the sheet: 1) an analytic G/G/1-inspired heuristic that approximates p95 using utilization amplification; 2) a fast Monte Carlo sim (discrete-event) seeded from trace histograms to compute empirical p50/p95/p99. Both should be available as tabs.
- Heuristic formula to try for naive_p95_queue_ms: alpha * (util/(1-util)) * mean_service_time where alpha is 0.6-1.4 tuned per trace. Documented in a cell so PMs can adjust.
- For short requests the effective service-time distribution is the min(service_time, T_short_slot_equivalent) when they use reservoir slots, so tail is thinner.

Operational heuristics and knobs (recommendations):
- Default reservoir_pct = clip(0.08, 0.25) depending on short_frac: if short_frac > 0.5 prefer 0.2; if short_frac < 0.15 prefer 0.07.
- slot_size_tok should be chosen as the 90th percentile of expected token-per-request for the long request cohort to avoid frequent splitting.
- concurrency_limit per node: choose small integers (4–16) matching GPU memory constraints; trading concurrency up increases context-switch and kernel overhead, so recalc kernel_overhead_ms when concurrency changes.
- Autoscaler policy suggestion: when short_frac spikes above 0.6 for >2 min, temporarily lower reservoir_pct (if short requests are dominating) to avoid under-utilization; conversely raise reservoir_pct if p95 short > target and utilization < 0.6.

Sim plan (spreadsheet + code hooks):
- Implement a lightweight discrete-event sim in Python that reads scenario rows from the sheet and outputs p50/p95/p99, slot utilization, wasted_reservoir_ms. Add a tab with summary metrics.
- Sim inputs: interarrival distribution per scenario (Poisson baseline + trace-shaped with peak-factor), length distribution (empirical hist buckets).
- Outputs to capture: per-request latency distribution, tail mass attributable to queueing behind longer requests, percent of reserved-slot idleness.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to account for KV-cache pressure and prefetched context across requests that share sessions? Current model treats every request independently; need trace-level session grouping to judge realistic packing gains.
- What is the correct tuning range for alpha in the heuristic queue formula across different arrival shapes? Need dataset of 50 trace-scenarios and per-scenario calibration.
- Integration with routing policies (cost-vs-latency): should we route short traffic to cheaper nodes without reservoir if p95 stays within SLA? Need cost-sla frontier cell in the sheet.
- Validate kernel_overhead_ms as concurrency changes; bench runs needed for the 2–16 concurrency sweep for both GPUs.

Next steps (concrete):
1) Add a "scenario playground" tab to the cost-model sheet with the columns above and the example rows.
2) Wire the sheet to a small sim (GH-serve/PR#489 as draft) and include a reproducible Python notebook that reads scenarios and emits p95 numbers.
3) Run 20 prod-trace seeds (one hour each) and populate calibration table for alpha and service-time variance.
4) Draft a short ops playbook for SRE on how to change reservoir_pct during incidents (runbook template included as a later tab).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally heuristic-first to give product teams knobs they can tune quickly. If we can validate with sim+traces and a handful of small bench runs, we can convert heuristics into controller policies in the autoscaler.
- Please add comments inline in the sheet rather than in drive doc to keep versioning tidy.

Unresolved: acceptable guardrails for reservoir_pct in multi-tenant clusters (we must not let one tenant pin >30% of slots across a node pool). Propose a hard cap in controller at 25% for now.

Appendix (quick glossary):
- slot: logical GPU packing container that can hold up to slot_size_tok tokens worth of requests per scheduling interval.
- reservoir: fraction of slots reserved for short/low-latency requests to reduce head-of-line blocking.
- short_frac: fraction of requests estimated to be latency-sensitive short requests.

End of draft.

-- marisol
